Company Overview
A ventro Motors Pvt. Ltd. is one of India’s rapidly growing automobile
manufacturers, renowned for its innovation in both conventional and alterna-
tive powertrain technologies. The company offers a comprehensive lineup of
passenger cars that includes petrol, diesel, electric, and hybrid variants.
Company History
A ventro Motors was founded in 2011 in Gurugram, Haryana, with a vision
to redefine the automotive landscape in India by offering a perfect blend of
technology, affordability, and sustainability. Starting with a compact team of
automobile enthusiasts, A ventro made its market debut in 2013 with the launch
of the A ventro Aero.
By 2015, A ventro established its state-of-the-art manufacturing facility in
Haryana and began expanding its product range. The company introduced
electric and hybrid models in 2017, making it one of the first Indian carmakers
to transition towards eco-friendly mobility solutions. The launch of the A ven-

electric and hybrid models in 2017, making it one of the first Indian carmakers
to transition towards eco-friendly mobility solutions. The launch of the A ven-

Despite industry headwinds, A ventro Motors achieved consistent growth. By

engagement and after-sales service. The company prides itself on fostering a

Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC): What is it &
How Does it Work?
Overview
Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC) is an advanced driver assistance system
(ADAS) designed to automatically adjust a vehicle’s cruising speed to maintain
a safe following distance from vehicles ahead. It’s an evolution of traditional
cruise control, offering greater safety, comfort, and convenience—especially in
highway and stop-and-go traﬀic scenarios.
What is Adaptive Cruise Control?
• T raditional Cruise Control : Maintains a set vehicle speed as chosen
by the driver.
• Adaptive Cruise Control : Uses sensors to detect vehicles ahead and
can increase, decrease, or maintain speed based on traﬀic conditions.
Key F unctions
1. Automatic Speed Regulation
Keeps the car traveling at a set speed until it detects a slower-moving
vehicle in its path.
2. Distance Monitoring & Maintenance
Constantly monitors the distance to the vehicle in front and adjusts speed
to maintain a safe, pre-set gap.

vehicle in its path.
2. Distance Monitoring & Maintenance
Constantly monitors the distance to the vehicle in front and adjusts speed
to maintain a safe, pre-set gap.
3. Automatic Braking and Acceleration
Decelerates when a slower vehicle is detected, and speeds back up to the
original set speed when the lane clears.
4. Stop & Go F unctionality (in advanced systems)
In heavy traﬀic, can bring the car to a complete stop and resume motion
as traﬀic moves.
How Does Adaptive Cruise Control Work?
Main Components
• Radar Sensors:
Typically mounted in the grille or front bumper to detect vehicles ahead
and measure their speed and distance.
• Lidar Sensors or Cameras:
Used in some systems for enhanced object detection and lane tracking.
1

• ECU (Electronic Control Unit):
Processes sensor data and commands the throttle and brakes as needed.
W orking Principle
1. Activation
The driver activates ACC and sets a desired speed and following distance
(often via steering wheel controls).
2. Monitoring
The system continuously scans the road ahead using radar, lidar, and/or
cameras.
3. Detection
• If the road ahead is clear, ACC maintains the set speed.
• If a slower vehicle is detected within the pre-set following distance,
ACC automatically reduces vehicle speed by controlling throttle and
brakes.
4. Control
• If the vehicle ahead speeds up, ACC accelerates (up to the set speed
limit).
• If the vehicle ahead slows down or stops, ACC decelerates and—if
equipped with stop & go—can bring the car to a halt.
5. Resuming
The system accelerates back to the set speed once the lane ahead is clear.
Example Scenario
• You set ACC to 100 km/h and the following distance to 2 seconds .
• A car merges ahead traveling at 80 km/h .

Example Scenario
• You set ACC to 100 km/h and the following distance to 2 seconds .
• A car merges ahead traveling at 80 km/h .
• ACC detects the vehicle and smoothly reduces your speed to maintain a
safe gap.
• When the lane ahead is clear, ACC returns your car to 100 km/h .
Advantages
• Safety: Reduces risk of rear-end collisions.
• Convenience: Less driver fatigue on long trips and in traﬀic jams.
• Eﬀiciency: Optimized speed and braking can improve fuel economy.
Limitations
• Sensor Limitations: May be affected by weather conditions, dirt, or
obstructions.
2

• Not a Substitute for Attention: The driver must remain alert and
ready to take control at all times.
Terminology
• ACC: Adaptive Cruise Control
• ADAS: Advanced Driver Assistance Systems

Adjusting the Seat Positions in A ventro Motors
Vehicles
Overview
Proper seat adjustment is essential for driving comfort, safety, and visibility.
A ventro Motors vehicles are equipped with manual and/or electronic seat ad-
justment controls, depending on the model and trim. This guide walks you
through adjusting your seat position for the safest and most comfortable driv-
ing experience.
Steps for Adjusting the Seat Positions
1. Adjusting the Seat Distance from the Pedals
• Locate the seat adjustment lever under the front edge of the seat.
• Pull the lever up to unlock the seat.
• Slide the seat forward or backward until your feet reach the pedals com-
fortably while keeping a slight bend at your knees.
• Release the lever to lock the seat in position.
• Gently rock the seat to ensure it is securely locked.
2. Adjusting the Seat Height (if equipped)
• Locate the seat height adjustment lever or electronic control (usually on
the side of the seat).

• Gently rock the seat to ensure it is securely locked.
2. Adjusting the Seat Height (if equipped)
• Locate the seat height adjustment lever or electronic control (usually on
the side of the seat).
• For manual systems, pump the lever up or down.
• For electronic systems, use the corresponding switch to raise or lower the
seat.
• Adjust until you have a clear view over the steering wheel and dashboard,
with adequate headspace.
3. Adjusting the Seat Backrest Angle
• Find the seat backrest adjustment lever or rotary knob at the side of the
seat.
• Lean forward slightly and pull or rotate the control to release the backrest.
• Adjust the backrest angle so you are sitting upright, with your shoulders
touching the seatback.
• The ideal angle is slightly reclined for comfort, but never more than 30°
from upright.
• Ensure the backrest is firmly locked in position before driving.
4. Adjusting the Headrest
• Hold both sides of the headrest.
1

• Press the adjustment button (usually at the base) and move the headrest
up or down.
• The top of the headrest should be level with the top of your head.
• The headrest should be as close to the back of your head as possible for
optimal safety.
5. Adjusting the Lumbar Support (if equipped)
• Use the lumbar support lever, dial, or electronic switch (side of seatback).
• Increase or decrease support as needed for comfort and spine alignment.
• Proper lumbar support helps reduce fatigue on long drives.
Tips for Safe Seat Adjustment
• Adjust your seat before starting the engine and while the car is stationary.
• Ensure all adjustments are firmly locked in place before driving.
• The distance between your chest and the steering wheel should be at least
25 cm (10 inches).
• Adjust the steering wheel if required, for optimal hand positioning.
• All passengers should also adjust their seats and headrests.

Adjusting the Steering Wheel
Proper steering wheel adjustment is essential for comfortable and safe driving.
Follow these steps to adjust your steering wheel for an optimal driving position.
Why Adjust the Steering Wheel?
• Comfort: Reduces fatigue during long drives.
• Control: Ensures effective steering and better handling.
• Safety: Ensures clear view of the instrument cluster and optimal airbag
positioning.
Types of Steering Wheel Adjustments
Most A ventro Motors vehicles come with either or both of the following:
• Tilt Adjustment: Allows the wheel to move up and down.
• T elescopic Adjustment: Allows the wheel to move closer or farther
from the driver.
Step-by-Step Guide
1. Park the V ehicle Safely
• Ensure the vehicle is on a flat surface and engage the parking brake.
• Turn off the engine for safety.
2. Locate the Adjustment Lever
• Look for the steering adjustment lever beneath or on the side of the steer-
ing column, usually beneath the wheel.
3. Release the Lever

2. Locate the Adjustment Lever
• Look for the steering adjustment lever beneath or on the side of the steer-
ing column, usually beneath the wheel.
3. Release the Lever
• Pull (or push, depending on the model) the adjustment lever to unlock
the steering wheel movement.
4. Adjust the Steering Wheel
• Tilt: Move the wheel up or down to a comfortable height.
• T elescopic: Pull the wheel towards you or push it away to set a comfort-
able distance.
• The steering wheel should not obstruct your view of the gauges.
1

5. Lock the Steering Wheel Position
• Once set, firmly push the adjustment lever back to the locked position.
6. Check Positioning
• With your back against the seat, extend your arms and rest your wrists
on top of the wheel; your elbows should be slightly bent.
• Ensure there is at least 25 cm (10 inches) between your chest and the
wheel (important for airbag safety).
• Confirm that all indicator lights and gauges are fully visible.
Tips
• Adjust your seat first before the steering wheel.
• If your vehicle has a heated steering wheel or steering wheel memory set-
tings, consult your owner’s manual for additional features.
• Never adjust the steering wheel while driving.
Troubleshooting
• Stuck Lever: Check for obstructions under/around the lever or consult
your nearest A ventro Service Center.
• Loose Wheel: Ensure the lever is locked; if the wheel remains loose, have
it inspected by a professional.

Advice for Pregnant Women While in a Car
Traveling by car is common during pregnancy, but it’s important to prioritize
safety and comfort for both mother and baby. Here’s a quick guide with essential
advice:
1. Always Wear Your Seat Belt Properly
• Three-Point Seat Belt : Use both lap and shoulder belts.
• Lap Belt : Position it under the belly , low on the hips, and across the
upper thighs. It should never go across your stomach.
• Shoulder Belt : Place it between the breasts and to the side of your
belly.
• Never Place Belt Behind Back or Under Arm : This reduces its
effectiveness and can be dangerous.
2. Adjust Your Seat for Maximum Comfort and Safety
• Sit Upright : Maintain a good posture—back straight, shoulders relaxed.
• Distance from Steering Wheel/Airbag : Adjust the seat so you’re as
far from the dashboard/steering wheel as possible, but still able to drive
comfortably.
• Tilt Steering Wheel Upwards : If possible, angle the steering wheel
towards your chest, not your belly.

Smartwatch connectivity allows you to interact with select vehicle functions
directly from your smartwatch. This may include lock/unlock, remote start,

A ventro Motors: How to Change a Tyre
Changing a flat tyre is a basic and essential automotive skill for every A ventro
Motor car owner. This guide will walk you through:
• Steps to change a tyre
• Where the spare tyre and toolkit is found in all A ventro models
• General tips and safety instructions
Where to Find the Spare Tyre & Toolkit in A ventro Models
Model Type Common Location of Spare Tyre & Toolkit
Hatchback Under the boot floor in the rear compartment
Sedan Under the boot floor in the trunk
SUV Under the boot floor or mounted underneath the rear of
the car
(All Models) Toolkit is usually secured next to the spare tyre or inside a
side panel of the boot/trunk
Note: All variants (Petrol/Diesel/Electric/Hybrid) follow the same compart-
ment arrangement.
Steps to Change a Tyre
1. Park Safely
• Pull over to a safe, flat location away from traﬀic.
• Turn on your hazard lights.
• Apply the handbrake.
• Place wheel wedges/blocks (if available) to prevent vehicle movement.

1. Park Safely
• Pull over to a safe, flat location away from traﬀic.
• Turn on your hazard lights.
• Apply the handbrake.
• Place wheel wedges/blocks (if available) to prevent vehicle movement.
2. Gather T ools
You will need: - Spare tyre (found as per table above) - Jack (usually in toolkit)
- Lug wrench (in toolkit) - Wheel wedges/blocks (optional) - Vehicle owner’s
manual (for reference)
3. Remove the Wheel Cover/Hubcap
• If your wheel has a cover, use the flat end of the wrench or the provided
lever to gently pry it off.
1

4. Loosen the Lug Nuts
• Use the lug wrench to turn the lug nuts counter-clockwise.
• Loosen them slightly – do not remove fully at this stage.
5. Lift the V ehicle with the Jack
• Position the jack under the jacking point nearest to the flat tyre. Refer to
your owner’s manual for the exact point.
• Raise the vehicle until the flat tyre is about 6 inches above the ground.
6. Remove the Lug Nuts and Tyre
• Unscrew the lug nuts completely.
• Remove the flat tyre and set it aside.
7. Mount the Spare Tyre
• Line up the holes and push the spare onto the hub.
• Replace the lug nuts and tighten them by hand.
8. Lower the V ehicle
• Carefully lower the car with the jack until the tyre touches the ground
firmly.
• Remove the jack.
9. Tighten the Lug Nuts
• Use the lug wrench to tighten the lug nuts in a star pattern to ensure even
pressure.
10. Replace the Hubcap or Wheel Cover (if applicable)
• Place the hubcap back onto the wheel.
11. Stow Equipment

Best Ways to Maintain Good Mileage
Achieving and maintaining good mileage is essential for saving fuel costs, re-
ducing environmental impact, and ensuring your vehicle’s long-term health.
Whether you drive a petrol, diesel, hybrid, or electric car from A ventro Mo-
tors, the following practices will help you get the most out of every journey.
1. Regular Maintenance
• F ollow Service Schedules: Stick to the manufacturer’s recommended
service intervals for oil changes, air filter replacements, and other checks.
• Use Genuine Parts: Always use genuine A ventro spare parts for optimal
performance (e.g., Air Filter, Spark Plug, Oil Filter).
2. Check Tyre Pressure
• Maintain Proper Pressure: Under-inflated tyres increase rolling resis-
tance and decrease mileage.
• Check Regularly: Inspect tyre pressure at least once a month and before
long trips.
3. Drive Smoothly
• A void Sudden Acceleration or Braking: Rapid changes waste fuel
and energy.

Best Ways to Use Your Car AC in All Seasons
For Aventro Motors Car Owners
Your vehicle’s air conditioning (AC) system is vital for comfort and safety
throughout the year. Whether it’s cooling in summer, defogging in monsoon,
or maintaining a pleasant environment in winter, knowing how to use the AC
eﬀiciently will extend system life and enhance your driving experience. Here’s
a guide to making the most of your AC system during every season.
Summer: Beat the Heat
1. V entilate First
- Before switching on the AC, roll down the windows and drive for a couple of
minutes to expel hot air.
- This makes the cabin cool down faster.
2. Use Recirculation Mode
- Turn on the AC and set it to “recirculate” once the cabin is cool. - This
prevents hot outside air from entering, making the system more effective.
3. Set the Right T emperature
- A void setting the thermostat to the lowest setting. 22-24°C (72-75°F) is usually
comfortable and easier on the compressor.
4. Regular Maintenance

Best Ways to Use Your headlamps Based on
Road, Traﬀic, and Climate
Driving conditions in India can vary dramatically depending on loca-
tion, weather, and traﬀic density . Y our headlamps (often referred to
as headlights)—play a crucial role not only for your visibility but for
the safety of everyone on the road. This guide from A ventro Motors
outlines the best practices for using your headlamps based on distinct
road, traﬀic, and climate scenarios.
1. Urban Roads with Heavy Traﬀic
• Use low beam: High beams can dazzle oncoming drivers and should be
avoided in city traﬀic.
• T urn on your headlamps in the evening/low light: Even if street
lights are present, using your headlamps enhances visibility.
• Hazards & signal lights: Use these for extra safety during sudden traﬀic
halts or in bumper-to-bumper situations.
2. Rural Roads & Highways
• Switch to high beam on poorly lit or empty stretches: Offers
extended visibility where street lighting is absent.

2. Rural Roads & Highways
• Switch to high beam on poorly lit or empty stretches: Offers
extended visibility where street lighting is absent.
• Dip your beam for oncoming vehicles: Always shift back to low beam
to avoid blinding other drivers.
• Check for road signs: Many rural roads feature animal crossings or
sharp curves—reduce speed and use dipped beams.
3. Foggy or Rainy Weather
• Always use low beam: High beams reflect off fog or rain, worsening
visibility.
• Activate fog lamps if available: These cut through the mist close to
the road.
• Use hazard lights only when stationary on road shoulder: Do not
use hazards while driving as it confuses other road users.
• Reduce speed and increase distance: Wet roads mean longer stopping
distances.

4. Dusty or Smoggy Conditions
• Low beam for better penetration: Cut through dust better and make
your car visible to others.
• Keep your headlamps and tail lamps clean: Dirt can cut your light
output significantly.
• Use headlamps during the day if visibility is poor: This helps both
you and others.
5. Twilight/Dawn and Overcast Days
• T urn on your headlamps even if it’s not dark: Light contrast is low
and reduces overall visibility.
• Switch on tail lamps as well: Make sure drivers behind you can see
your vehicle.
6. Hilly and Winding Roads
• Always use dipper at turns and blind spots: Alert oncoming vehicles
of your presence.
• High beam for long stretches at night: But revert to low beam for
sharp turns or when climbing gradients.
7. Night Driving
• Regularly alternate between high and low beam: Use high for
extended visibility and low when another vehicle is near.
• A void using only parking lights: These are not suﬀicient for visibility
or indication.

When your A ventro vehicle’s engine refuses to start, it can be frustrating. Use
this step-by-step guide to help diagnose and resolve the problem, or to gather
information before contacting an A ventro Service Center.

• Gear Position: Ensure the car is in ‘Park’ (automatic) or ‘Neutral’ (man-
ual).
• Steering Lock: Gently turn the steering wheel while turning the key if
steering is locked.
• Key/Start Button: Switch ignition off and retry. For push-button start,
press brake/clutch while starting.
2. Battery Check
• Symptoms: No lights/display, slow/absent cranking sounds, clicking
noise.
• Actions:
– Inspect dashboard for dim or no lights.
– Try using headlights or infotainment; if dim or off, battery may be
the culprit.
– If available, try jump-starting with a healthy battery.
– For Electric variants: Ensure Battery Pack has adequate charge. At-
tempt Fast Charging if possible.

Opening the fuel knob (fuel cap) on your A ventro vehicle is a simple process.
Follow these steps to ensure safe and easy access when you need to refuel:
Steps to Open the Fuel Knob
1. Park & Switch Off the Engine
• Ensure your car is completely stopped and the engine is turned off.
• Engage the parking brake for safety.
2. Locate the F uel Knob Release Lever
• The fuel knob release lever is typically found:
– On the driver’s side floor, near the seat or door.
– In some models, it may be on the dashboard or central console.
3. Pull the Release Lever
• Pull up or push the lever labelled with a fuel pump icon .
• You may hear a click indicating the fuel lid has been released.
4. Exit the Car
• Step out of the vehicle and go to the side where the fuel lid (fuel
door) is located.
5. Open the F uel Lid
• Gently open the fuel lid.
• You’ll now see the fuel knob (fuel cap).
6. T urn and Remove the F uel Knob

How to Open the Hood of an A ventro Vehicle
Opening the hood of your A ventro car is a simple process that gives you access
to the engine compartment for checks and maintenance. Follow these steps:
Steps to Open the Hood
1. Park the Car Safely
• Ensure your car is parked on a level surface.
• Turn off the engine and engage the parking brake.
2. Locate the Hood Release Lever
• The hood release lever is usually located under the dashboard, to the
right or left of the driver’s seat (near the footwell).
• Look for a lever with a hood icon (it may show a car with an open
hood).
3. Pull the Hood Release Lever
• Pull the lever firmly. You should hear a slight click as the hood pops
up a little.
4. Move to the F ront of the Car
• Go to the front of the vehicle.
• The hood will now be slightly raised.
5. Find the Secondary Latch
• Slide your hand under the center front edge of the hood.
• Feel for the secondary latch (usually a small lever or tab).

manual).
• Press the brake pedal (and the clutch for manual transmission).
A. Petrol & Diesel Models
With Standard Key Ignition

steering column).

starts.

The instrument cluster in A ventro Motors vehicles is designed to inform the

to avoid engine damage.

brake pads, or handbrake engaged.

Lane Keeping Assist System (LKAS): Overview
& Functionality
What is Lane Keeping Assist System (LKAS)?
Lane Keeping Assist System (LKAS) is an advanced driver assistance
system (ADAS) designed to enhance road safety by helping drivers keep their
vehicles within marked lane boundaries. LKAS is commonly found in modern
vehicles and acts as a semi-autonomous feature, working alongside the driver to
prevent unintentional lane departure.
Why is LKAS Important?
• Reduces Accidents: Lane departures are a major cause of road acci-
dents, especially due to driver drowsiness, distraction, or inattention.
• Enhances Safety: By consistently monitoring the vehicle’s position,
LKAS can help avoid unintended drift into adjacent lanes.
• Supports the Driver: LKAS provides gentle steering inputs or alerts,
acting as a backup to human oversight.
How Does Lane Keeping Assist System Work?
1. Sensing the Lane
• Cameras: Typically, a forward-facing camera mounted near the rear-view

acting as a backup to human oversight.
How Does Lane Keeping Assist System Work?
1. Sensing the Lane
• Cameras: Typically, a forward-facing camera mounted near the rear-view
mirror scans the road ahead for lane markings (white/yellow lines).
• Sensors: Some advanced systems use a combination of cameras, LIDAR,
or radar to enhance accuracy in different lighting and weather conditions.
2. Processing the Image
• The camera/system detects lane boundaries by analyzing road markings
in real-time.
• On-board computers determine if the vehicle is unintentionally veering out
of its lane.
3. W arning the Driver
• If the vehicle starts drifting toward a lane marking without indicating
(using a turn signal), the system may give audible or visual warnings (e.g.,
a beep, steering wheel vibration, or dashboard alert).
1

4. Active Assistance
• If the driver doesn’t respond to the warnings, LKAS can automatically
provide gentle steering input to guide the car back toward the center of
the lane.
• Some systems may also use selective braking on one side of the vehicle to
assist in correcting the course.
Key Features
• Automatic Steering Correction: Minor, smooth counter-steering to
stay centered in the lane.
• Customizable Sensitivity: Most systems allow drivers to adjust the
responsiveness or can be switched off.
• Integrated with Other Systems: Often works alongside Lane Depar-
ture Warning (LDW) and Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC).
Limitations & Considerations
• Reliant on Lane Markings: LKAS requires clear, visible lane lines;
performance may degrade in poor weather, faded markings, or during
road construction.
• Not a Substitute for Attention: LKAS assists, but the driver must
keep hands on the wheel and remain attentive at all times.
• May Not Operate at All Speeds: Some systems only work above

• Not a Substitute for Attention: LKAS assists, but the driver must
keep hands on the wheel and remain attentive at all times.
• May Not Operate at All Speeds: Some systems only work above
certain speeds (e.g., above 60 km/h).
Typical LKAS Workflow
1. V ehicle Camera Detects Lane
2. Control Unit Monitors Position Relative to Lane Marks
3. If Drift Detected: System Alerts Driver
4. If No Response: System Gently Steers Vehicle Back to Lane Center
Conclusion
Lane Keeping Assist System is a valuable safety technology that helps prevent
unintentional lane departures, reducing the risk of side-swipe collisions and road
departure accidents. While it offers significant safety benefits, it is not an au-
tonomous driving system—driver vigilance and control remain essential.
2

Opening and Closing the Boot
Opening the Boot
There are several ways you can open the boot (trunk) of your A ventro vehicle,
depending on the model and features equipped:
1. Manual Release (Lever/Button)
• Locate the boot release lever or button inside the vehicle.
– Usually found near the driver’s seat or on the driver’s side door panel.
• Pull the lever or press the button.
– You’ll hear a click indicating the boot is unlocked.
• Go to the rear of the vehicle and lift the boot lid upwards to open.
2. Remote Key F ob
• Press and hold the boot release button on your vehicle’s remote key fob.
• The boot will unlock and, on some models, may open slightly for you to
lift.
3. Exterior Button or Handle
• With the vehicle unlocked, press the soft-touch button or lift the handle
located just above the number plate or under the boot lid.
• Lift the boot gently to open.
4. Hands-F ree Option (If Equipped)
• With the key fob in your possession, stand behind the boot and make a

located just above the number plate or under the boot lid.
• Lift the boot gently to open.
4. Hands-F ree Option (If Equipped)
• With the key fob in your possession, stand behind the boot and make a
gentle kicking motion under the center of the rear bumper (sensor area).
• Wait for a few seconds; the boot will unlatch automatically. Lift to open.
Closing the Boot
1. Manual Closing
• Grip the inner handle or any designated area on the inside of the boot lid.
• Pull the boot lid down smoothly and press gently until you hear it latch.
2. Electrically Assisted/T ailgate Models (If Equipped)
• Press the boot’s close button (located on the edge of the boot lid).
• The lid will automatically close and latch securely.
1

3. Cautions When Closing
• Make sure there are no obstructions or luggage sticking out.
• Ensure all hands and fingers are away from the boot area before closing.
• Do not slam the boot lid; close it with a gentle but firm push.
Note:
If the boot does not open or close properly, check if the vehicle is in
‘Valet Mode’ or if the child safety lock for the boot is engaged. For
electrically operated boots, ensure the battery has suﬀicient charge.
Need Help?
If you experience any issues with your boot mechanism, please visit the nearest
A ventro Service Center or contact A ventro Motors Pvt. Ltd.

Driving safely is crucial for protecting yourself, your passengers, and others on

□ Ensure you are well-rested and not under the influence of alcohol, drugs,

□ Perform a quick walk-around inspection of the car:

□ No visible leaks or loose parts
□ Adjust your seat, headrest, and mirrors for comfort and proper view.
□ Fasten your seat belt and ensure all passengers are buckled up.
□ Check that all doors are properly closed and locked.
□ Clear the windshield and mirrors of obstructions/dirt.
□ Secure any loose items in the vehicle.

□ Ensure the gear is in neutral/park.
□ Press the brake pedal before starting.

Traction Control
What is Traction Control?
T raction Control is a vehicle safety feature designed to prevent the loss of
traction (grip) of the driven road wheels, which can occur during acceleration.
By detecting when one or more wheels are slipping, the system automatically
applies the brakes or reduces engine power to maintain optimal grip, especially
on slippery surfaces.
How Does Traction Control Work?
Traction control systems are usually integrated with a car’s anti-lock braking
system (ABS) and electronic stability control (ESC). The basic operation in-
volves:
1. Sensors detect when a wheel is spinning faster than others (indicating
loss of traction).
2. Electronic Control Unit (ECU) receives data from sensors and deter-
mines the appropriate intervention.
3. Intervention:
• Braking: The system applies brakes to the slipping wheel(s).
• Engine Control: The ECU may reduce engine power or throttle
input to minimize wheel spin.
Key Components

3. Intervention:
• Braking: The system applies brakes to the slipping wheel(s).
• Engine Control: The ECU may reduce engine power or throttle
input to minimize wheel spin.
Key Components
• Wheel Speed Sensors: Monitor the rotational speed of each wheel.
• ECU (Electronic Control Unit): Processes sensor data and manages
interventions.
• Braking Mechanism: Engages individual brakes as needed.
• Throttle Control (in advanced systems): Modulates engine power.
Benefits of Traction Control
• Improved Safety: Helps maintain control during acceleration on wet,
icy, or loose surfaces.
• Reduced Wheel Spin: Minimizes tire wear and prevents excessive wheel
spin.
• Enhanced Stability: Works in tandem with ABS and ESC for overall
vehicle stability.
1

When Does Traction Control Activate?
• Accelerating quickly on wet, icy, sandy, or gravelly surfaces.
• When one or more wheels begin to slip or lose contact with the road.
• During sharp turns, especially in low-traction conditions.
Limitations of Traction Control
• Cannot increase tire traction: Only manages existing traction without
creating more.
• Limited usefulness on all surfaces: May not be as effective on ex-
tremely slippery or uneven terrains.
• Not a substitute for safe driving practices: Drivers should still use
caution in poor conditions.
Traction Control in A ventro Motors Cars
Most modern vehicles, including A ventro Motors models across Hatchback,
Sedan, and SUV variants, are equipped with traction control as standard or
optional, especially in ZX or higher trim levels. This is part of A ventro’s
commitment to vehicle safety and performance under varied driving conditions.

braking situations. By maintaining tractive contact with the road surface, ABS
enhances vehicle control and reduces stopping distances on both wet and dry
surfaces.
Key Purpose of ABS
• Prevents wheel lock-up during sudden or hard braking.
• Maintains steering control, allowing the driver to maneuver the vehicle
while braking.
• Reduces the risk of skidding or uncontrolled vehicle movement.
How Does ABS Work?
ABS operates using a combination of sensors, valves, and electronic control units.
Here is a simplified step-by-step process:

speed of the wheels continuously.

• If any sensor detects a sudden decrease in wheel speed (indicating
potential lock-up), the ABS system is activated.
2.

• The ECU receives data from the wheel speed sensors.

brake pressure through a modulator.

cession, ABS prevents the wheels from locking up .
• The driver can continue to steer effectively even during heavy brak-
ing.

cles while braking hard.
• Shorter Stopping Distance: Especially on slippery or wet roads, ABS
can reduce stopping distances.

Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC): What is it & How Does it Work?

Overview

Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC) is an advanced driver assistance system (ADAS) designed to automatically adjust a vehicle’s cruising speed to maintain a safe following distance from vehicles ahead. It’s an evolution of traditional cruise control, offering greater safety, comfort, and convenience—especially in highway and stop-and-go traffic scenarios.



What is Adaptive Cruise Control?

Traditional Cruise Control: Maintains a set vehicle speed as chosen by the driver.

Adaptive Cruise Control: Uses sensors to detect vehicles ahead and can increase, decrease, or maintain speed based on traffic conditions.

Key Functions

Automatic Speed Regulation
Keeps the car traveling at a set speed until it detects a slower-moving vehicle in its path.

Distance Monitoring & Maintenance
Constantly monitors the distance to the vehicle in front and adjusts speed to maintain a safe, pre-set gap.

Distance Monitoring & Maintenance
Constantly monitors the distance to the vehicle in front and adjusts speed to maintain a safe, pre-set gap.

Automatic Braking and Acceleration
Decelerates when a slower vehicle is detected, and speeds back up to the original set speed when the lane clears.

Stop & Go Functionality (in advanced systems)
In heavy traffic, can bring the car to a complete stop and resume motion as traffic moves.



How Does Adaptive Cruise Control Work?

Main Components

Radar Sensors:
Typically mounted in the grille or front bumper to detect vehicles ahead and measure their speed and distance.

Lidar Sensors or Cameras:
Used in some systems for enhanced object detection and lane tracking.

ECU (Electronic Control Unit):
Processes sensor data and commands the throttle and brakes as needed.

Working Principle

Activation
The driver activates ACC and sets a desired speed and following distance (often via steering wheel controls).

Working Principle

Activation
The driver activates ACC and sets a desired speed and following distance (often via steering wheel controls).

Monitoring
The system continuously scans the road ahead using radar, lidar, and/or cameras.

Detection

If the road ahead is clear, ACC maintains the set speed.

If a slower vehicle is detected within the pre-set following distance, ACC automatically reduces vehicle speed by controlling throttle and brakes.

Control

If the vehicle ahead speeds up, ACC accelerates (up to the set speed limit).

If the vehicle ahead slows down or stops, ACC decelerates and—if equipped with stop & go—can bring the car to a halt.

Resuming
The system accelerates back to the set speed once the lane ahead is clear.

Example Scenario

You set ACC to 100 km/h and the following distance to 2 seconds.

A car merges ahead traveling at 80 km/h.

ACC detects the vehicle and smoothly reduces your speed to maintain a safe gap.

ACC detects the vehicle and smoothly reduces your speed to maintain a safe gap.

When the lane ahead is clear, ACC returns your car to 100 km/h.



Advantages

Safety: Reduces risk of rear-end collisions.

Convenience: Less driver fatigue on long trips and in traffic jams.

Efficiency: Optimized speed and braking can improve fuel economy.

Limitations

Sensor Limitations: May be affected by weather conditions, dirt, or obstructions.

Not a Substitute for Attention: The driver must remain alert and ready to take control at all times.

Terminology

ACC: Adaptive Cruise Control

ADAS: Advanced Driver Assistance Systems

Advice for Pregnant Women While in a Car

Traveling by car is common during pregnancy, but it’s important to prioritize safety and comfort for both mother and baby. Here’s a quick guide with essential advice:



1. Always Wear Your Seat Belt Properly

Three-Point Seat Belt: Use both lap and shoulder belts.

Lap Belt: Position it under the belly, low on the hips, and across the upper thighs. It should never go across your stomach.

Shoulder Belt: Place it between the breasts and to the side of your belly.

Never Place Belt Behind Back or Under Arm: This reduces its effectiveness and can be dangerous.



2. Adjust Your Seat for Maximum Comfort and Safety

Sit Upright: Maintain a good posture—back straight, shoulders relaxed.

Distance from Steering Wheel/Airbag: Adjust the seat so you’re as far from the dashboard/steering wheel as possible, but still able to drive comfortably.

Tilt Steering Wheel Upwards: If possible, angle the steering wheel towards your chest, not your belly.

3. Remove the Wheel Cover/Hubcap

If your wheel has a cover, use the flat end of the wrench or the provided lever to gently pry it off.

4. Loosen the Lug Nuts

Use the lug wrench to turn the lug nuts counter-clockwise.

Loosen them slightly – do not remove fully at this stage.

5. Lift the Vehicle with the Jack

Position the jack under the jacking point nearest to the flat tyre. Refer to your owner’s manual for the exact point.

Raise the vehicle until the flat tyre is about 6 inches above the ground.

6. Remove the Lug Nuts and Tyre

Unscrew the lug nuts completely.

metadata.source: C:\Users\fahad\Desktop\Uni\Projects\VoiceKit\business\knowledge_base\Aventro Motors\docx\Aventro Motors- How to Change a Tyre.docx

text:
Raise the vehicle until the flat tyre is about 6 inches above the ground.

6. Remove the Lug Nuts and Tyre

Unscrew the lug nuts completely.

Remove the flat tyre and set it aside.

7. Mount the Spare Tyre

Line up the holes and push the spare onto the hub.

Replace the lug nuts and tighten them by hand.

8. Lower the Vehicle

Carefully lower the car with the jack until the tyre touches the ground firmly.

Remove the jack.

9. Tighten the Lug Nuts

Use the lug wrench to tighten the lug nuts in a star pattern to ensure even pressure.

10. Replace the Hubcap or Wheel Cover (if applicable)

Place the hubcap back onto the wheel.

11. Stow Equipment

Put the flat tyre, jack, and tools back in their compartments.

Double check everything is secure.



Safety & Tips

Never change a tyre on a slope or close to traffic.

Use hazard warning triangle if available.

After installation, drive slowly and get the spare tyre pressure checked at the nearest Aventro Service Center.

Best Ways to Use Your Car AC in All Seasons

For Aventro Motors Car Owners



Your vehicle’s air conditioning (AC) system is vital for comfort and safety throughout the year. Whether it’s cooling in summer, defogging in monsoon, or maintaining a pleasant environment in winter, knowing how to use the AC efficiently will extend system life and enhance your driving experience. Here’s a guide to making the most of your AC system during every season.



Summer: Beat the Heat

1. Ventilate First
- Before switching on the AC, roll down the windows and drive for a couple of minutes to expel hot air.
- This makes the cabin cool down faster.

2. Use Recirculation Mode
- Turn on the AC and set it to “recirculate” once the cabin is cool. - This prevents hot outside air from entering, making the system more effective.

3. Set the Right Temperature
- Avoid setting the thermostat to the lowest setting. 22-24°C (72-75°F) is usually comfortable and easier on the compressor.

3. Set the Right Temperature
- Avoid setting the thermostat to the lowest setting. 22-24°C (72-75°F) is usually comfortable and easier on the compressor.

4. Regular Maintenance
- Clean or replace the cabin air filter. - Get your AC system inspected and refrigerant topped up at an Aventro Service Center before summer starts.



Monsoon: Fight Humidity and Fog

1. Use AC for Defogging
- Turn on the AC with the blower directed at the windshield to quickly clear fog. - Use the “fresh air” mode for a few minutes to reduce internal humidity.

2. Don’t Use Recirculate Mode Continuously
- Constant recirculation during rains may increase humidity inside, causing more fogging.

3. Keep Windows Closed
- Prevent water and more humidity from entering the cabin.



Winter: Comfort with Care

1. Run the AC Regularly
- Turn on the AC for at least 10 minutes once a week, even in winter.
- This keeps seals lubricated and prevents mold in the system.

Best Ways to Use Your headlamps Based on Road, Traffic, and Climate

Driving conditions in India can vary dramatically depending on location, weather, and traffic density. Your headlamps (often referred to as headlights)—play a crucial role not only for your visibility but for the safety of everyone on the road. This guide from Aventro Motors outlines the best practices for using your headlamps based on distinct road, traffic, and climate scenarios.



1. Urban Roads with Heavy Traffic

Use low beam: High beams can dazzle oncoming drivers and should be avoided in city traffic.

Turn on your headlamps in the evening/low light: Even if street lights are present, using your headlamps enhances visibility.

Hazards & signal lights: Use these for extra safety during sudden traffic halts or in bumper-to-bumper situations.



2. Rural Roads & Highways

Switch to high beam on poorly lit or empty stretches: Offers extended visibility where street lighting is absent.

metadata.source: C:\Users\fahad\Desktop\Uni\Projects\VoiceKit\business\knowledge_base\Aventro Motors\docx\Best Ways to Use Your headlamps.docx

text:
2. Rural Roads & Highways

Switch to high beam on poorly lit or empty stretches: Offers extended visibility where street lighting is absent.

Dip your beam for oncoming vehicles: Always shift back to low beam to avoid blinding other drivers.

Check for road signs: Many rural roads feature animal crossings or sharp curves—reduce speed and use dipped beams.



3. Foggy or Rainy Weather

Always use low beam: High beams reflect off fog or rain, worsening visibility.

Activate fog lamps if available: These cut through the mist close to the road.

Use hazard lights only when stationary on road shoulder: Do not use hazards while driving as it confuses other road users.

Reduce speed and increase distance: Wet roads mean longer stopping distances.



4. Dusty or Smoggy Conditions

Low beam for better penetration: Cut through dust better and make your car visible to others.

Keep your headlamps and tail lamps clean: Dirt can cut your light output significantly.

Low beam for better penetration: Cut through dust better and make your car visible to others.

Keep your headlamps and tail lamps clean: Dirt can cut your light output significantly.

Use headlamps during the day if visibility is poor: This helps both you and others.



5. Twilight/Dawn and Overcast Days

Turn on your headlamps even if it’s not dark: Light contrast is low and reduces overall visibility.

Switch on tail lamps as well: Make sure drivers behind you can see your vehicle.



6. Hilly and Winding Roads

Always use dipper at turns and blind spots: Alert oncoming vehicles of your presence.

High beam for long stretches at night: But revert to low beam for sharp turns or when climbing gradients.



7. Night Driving

Regularly alternate between high and low beam: Use high for extended visibility and low when another vehicle is near.

Avoid using only parking lights: These are not sufficient for visibility or indication.

Drive cautiously: Traction and braking are affected.

Clean headlamp lenses regularly to maximize light output.

Replace bulbs periodically as they dim with age, even if they haven’t fused.

Check all lighting systems before monsoons or long journeys.

Steering Lock: Gently turn the steering wheel while turning the key if steering is locked.

Key/Start Button: Switch ignition off and retry. For push-button start, press brake/clutch while starting.

Actions:

Inspect dashboard for dim or no lights.

Try using headlights or infotainment; if dim or off, battery may be the culprit.

If available, try jump-starting with a healthy battery.

For Electric variants: Ensure Battery Pack has adequate charge. Attempt Fast Charging if possible.

Lane Keeping Assist System (LKAS): Overview & Functionality

What is Lane Keeping Assist System (LKAS)?

Lane Keeping Assist System (LKAS) is an advanced driver assistance system (ADAS) designed to enhance road safety by helping drivers keep their vehicles within marked lane boundaries. LKAS is commonly found in modern vehicles and acts as a semi-autonomous feature, working alongside the driver to prevent unintentional lane departure.



Why is LKAS Important?

Reduces Accidents: Lane departures are a major cause of road accidents, especially due to driver drowsiness, distraction, or inattention.

Enhances Safety: By consistently monitoring the vehicle’s position, LKAS can help avoid unintended drift into adjacent lanes.

Supports the Driver: LKAS provides gentle steering inputs or alerts, acting as a backup to human oversight.



How Does Lane Keeping Assist System Work?

1. Sensing the Lane

Supports the Driver: LKAS provides gentle steering inputs or alerts, acting as a backup to human oversight.



How Does Lane Keeping Assist System Work?

1. Sensing the Lane

Cameras: Typically, a forward-facing camera mounted near the rear-view mirror scans the road ahead for lane markings (white/yellow lines).

Sensors: Some advanced systems use a combination of cameras, LIDAR, or radar to enhance accuracy in different lighting and weather conditions.

2. Processing the Image

The camera/system detects lane boundaries by analyzing road markings in real-time.

On-board computers determine if the vehicle is unintentionally veering out of its lane.

3. Warning the Driver

If the vehicle starts drifting toward a lane marking without indicating (using a turn signal), the system may give audible or visual warnings (e.g., a beep, steering wheel vibration, or dashboard alert).

4. Active Assistance

4. Active Assistance

If the driver doesn’t respond to the warnings, LKAS can automatically provide gentle steering input to guide the car back toward the center of the lane.

Some systems may also use selective braking on one side of the vehicle to assist in correcting the course.



Key Features

Automatic Steering Correction: Minor, smooth counter-steering to stay centered in the lane.

Customizable Sensitivity: Most systems allow drivers to adjust the responsiveness or can be switched off.

Integrated with Other Systems: Often works alongside Lane Departure Warning (LDW) and Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC).



Limitations & Considerations

Reliant on Lane Markings: LKAS requires clear, visible lane lines; performance may degrade in poor weather, faded markings, or during road construction.

Not a Substitute for Attention: LKAS assists, but the driver must keep hands on the wheel and remain attentive at all times.

Not a Substitute for Attention: LKAS assists, but the driver must keep hands on the wheel and remain attentive at all times.

May Not Operate at All Speeds: Some systems only work above certain speeds (e.g., above 60 km/h).



Typical LKAS Workflow

Vehicle Camera Detects Lane

Control Unit Monitors Position Relative to Lane Marks

If Drift Detected: System Alerts Driver

If No Response: System Gently Steers Vehicle Back to Lane Center



Conclusion

Lane Keeping Assist System is a valuable safety technology that helps prevent unintentional lane departures, reducing the risk of side-swipe collisions and road departure accidents. While it offers significant safety benefits, it is not an autonomous driving system—driver vigilance and control remain essential.



References/For More Information
- NHTSA on Lane Assistance Features - IIHS: Lane Departure Prevention

Driving safely is crucial for protecting yourself, your passengers, and others on the road. Before and while you drive, follow this checklist to ensure you’re operating your vehicle responsibly.



1. Before You Start the Car

☐ Ensure you are well-rested and not under the influence of alcohol, drugs, or strong medication.

☐ Check weather and road conditions.

☐ Perform a quick walk-around inspection of the car:

☐ Tire condition and pressure

☐ All lights functioning (headlights, brake lights, indicators)

☐ No visible leaks or loose parts

☐ Adjust your seat, headrest, and mirrors for comfort and proper view.

☐ Fasten your seat belt and ensure all passengers are buckled up.

☐ Check that all doors are properly closed and locked.

☐ Clear the windshield and mirrors of obstructions/dirt.

☐ Secure any loose items in the vehicle.



2. Starting the Car

☐ Ensure the gear is in neutral/park.

☐ Press the brake pedal before starting.

☐ Secure any loose items in the vehicle.

3. While Driving

☐ Use headlights in low light, rain, or fog.

☐ Continuously check rear-view and side mirrors.

☐ Yield to pedestrians and emergency vehicles.

Traction Control

What is Traction Control?

Traction Control is a vehicle safety feature designed to prevent the loss of traction (grip) of the driven road wheels, which can occur during acceleration. By detecting when one or more wheels are slipping, the system automatically applies the brakes or reduces engine power to maintain optimal grip, especially on slippery surfaces.



How Does Traction Control Work?

Traction control systems are usually integrated with a car’s anti-lock braking system (ABS) and electronic stability control (ESC). The basic operation involves:

Sensors detect when a wheel is spinning faster than others (indicating loss of traction).

Electronic Control Unit (ECU) receives data from sensors and determines the appropriate intervention.

Intervention:

Braking: The system applies brakes to the slipping wheel(s).

Engine Control: The ECU may reduce engine power or throttle input to minimize wheel spin.



Key Components

Intervention:

Braking: The system applies brakes to the slipping wheel(s).

Engine Control: The ECU may reduce engine power or throttle input to minimize wheel spin.



Key Components

Wheel Speed Sensors: Monitor the rotational speed of each wheel.

ECU (Electronic Control Unit): Processes sensor data and manages interventions.

Braking Mechanism: Engages individual brakes as needed.

Throttle Control (in advanced systems): Modulates engine power.



Benefits of Traction Control

Improved Safety: Helps maintain control during acceleration on wet, icy, or loose surfaces.

Reduced Wheel Spin: Minimizes tire wear and prevents excessive wheel spin.

Enhanced Stability: Works in tandem with ABS and ESC for overall vehicle stability.



When Does Traction Control Activate?

Accelerating quickly on wet, icy, sandy, or gravelly surfaces.

When one or more wheels begin to slip or lose contact with the road.

During sharp turns, especially in low-traction conditions.

Accelerating quickly on wet, icy, sandy, or gravelly surfaces.

When one or more wheels begin to slip or lose contact with the road.

During sharp turns, especially in low-traction conditions.



Limitations of Traction Control

Cannot increase tire traction: Only manages existing traction without creating more.

Limited usefulness on all surfaces: May not be as effective on extremely slippery or uneven terrains.

Not a substitute for safe driving practices: Drivers should still use caution in poor conditions.



Traction Control in Aventro Motors Cars

Most modern vehicles, including Aventro Motors models across Hatchback, Sedan, and SUV variants, are equipped with traction control as standard or optional, especially in ZX or higher trim levels. This is part of Aventro’s commitment to vehicle safety and performance under varied driving conditions.



Traction Control Indicator Light

Traction Control Indicator Light

The dashboard display will often include a traction control symbol: - Illuminates briefly when system is engaged or if road conditions are slippery. - Constant illumination may indicate a fault in the traction control system; service is recommended at an authorized Aventro Service Center.



Maintenance & Service

What is ABS (Anti-lock Braking System) and How Does It Work?

Introduction

ABS stands for Anti-lock Braking System. It is a vital safety feature in modern vehicles, designed to prevent the wheels from locking up during emergency braking situations. By maintaining tractive contact with the road surface, ABS enhances vehicle control and reduces stopping distances on both wet and dry surfaces.



Key Purpose of ABS

Prevents wheel lock-up during sudden or hard braking.

Maintains steering control, allowing the driver to maneuver the vehicle while braking.

Reduces the risk of skidding or uncontrolled vehicle movement.



How Does ABS Work?

ABS operates using a combination of sensors, valves, and electronic control units. Here is a simplified step-by-step process:

Wheel Speed Sensors

ABS uses sensors located at each wheel to monitor the rotational speed of the wheels continuously.

Wheel Speed Sensors

ABS uses sensors located at each wheel to monitor the rotational speed of the wheels continuously.

If any sensor detects a sudden decrease in wheel speed (indicating potential lock-up), the ABS system is activated.

Electronic Control Unit (ECU)

The ECU receives data from the wheel speed sensors.

When it detects a wheel about to lock, it controls the hydraulic brake pressure through a modulator.

Hydraulic Valves/Modulator

These valves rapidly increase or decrease brake pressure to each wheel as needed.

This process occurs many times per second (often felt as a “pulsating” brake pedal).

Brake Release and Reapplication

By releasing and then reapplying the brakes repeatedly in quick succession, ABS prevents the wheels from locking up.

The driver can continue to steer effectively even during heavy braking.



Advantages of ABS

Improved Steering Control: Allows the driver to steer around obstacles while braking hard.

The driver can continue to steer effectively even during heavy braking.



Advantages of ABS

Improved Steering Control: Allows the driver to steer around obstacles while braking hard.

Shorter Stopping Distance: Especially on slippery or wet roads, ABS can reduce stopping distances.

Reduced Tire Wear: Prevents flat-spotting of tires due to skidding.



When is ABS Most Useful?

Wet or icy roads

Gravel or loose road surfaces

Emergency stops requiring both braking and steering maneuvers



Common Misconceptions

ABS does not decrease stopping distance in all conditions, especially on loose gravel or snow where locked wheels can help build up material in front of the tires.

ABS is not a substitute for safe driving or maintaining a safe following distance.



How ABS Feels in Action

During hard braking, you may feel a pulsating sensation in the brake pedal.

This is normal and indicates that the ABS is actively working.

How ABS Feels in Action

During hard braking, you may feel a pulsating sensation in the brake pedal.

This is normal and indicates that the ABS is actively working.

Do not pump the brakes; instead, apply firm, continuous pressure.



Conclusion

Anti-lock Braking System (ABS) is a critical automotive safety technology that saves lives by helping drivers maintain control of their vehicles in emergency situations. By understanding how ABS works, drivers can maximize its benefits and contribute to safer roads.

Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC): What is it & How Does it Work?

Overview

Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC) is an advanced driver assistance system (ADAS) designed to automatically adjust a vehicle’s cruising speed to maintain a safe following distance from vehicles ahead. It’s an evolution of traditional cruise control, offering greater safety, comfort, and convenience—especially in highway and stop-and-go traffic scenarios.

What is Adaptive Cruise Control?

Traditional Cruise Control: Maintains a set vehicle speed as chosen by the driver.

Adaptive Cruise Control: Uses sensors to detect vehicles ahead and can increase, decrease, or maintain speed based on traffic conditions.

Key Functions

Automatic Speed Regulation Keeps the car traveling at a set speed until it detects a slower-moving vehicle in its path.

Distance Monitoring & Maintenance Constantly monitors the distance to the vehicle in front and adjusts speed to maintain a safe, pre-set gap.

Distance Monitoring & Maintenance Constantly monitors the distance to the vehicle in front and adjusts speed to maintain a safe, pre-set gap.

Automatic Braking and Acceleration Decelerates when a slower vehicle is detected, and speeds back up to the original set speed when the lane clears.

Stop & Go Functionality (in advanced systems) In heavy traffic, can bring the car to a complete stop and resume motion as traffic moves.

How Does Adaptive Cruise Control Work?

Main Components

Radar Sensors: Typically mounted in the grille or front bumper to detect vehicles ahead and measure their speed and distance.

Lidar Sensors or Cameras: Used in some systems for enhanced object detection and lane tracking.

ECU (Electronic Control Unit): Processes sensor data and commands the throttle and brakes as needed.

Working Principle

Activation The driver activates ACC and sets a desired speed and following distance (often via steering wheel controls).

Working Principle

Activation The driver activates ACC and sets a desired speed and following distance (often via steering wheel controls).

Monitoring The system continuously scans the road ahead using radar, lidar, and/or cameras.

Detection

If the road ahead is clear, ACC maintains the set speed.

If a slower vehicle is detected within the pre-set following distance, ACC automatically reduces vehicle speed by controlling throttle and brakes.

Control

If the vehicle ahead speeds up, ACC accelerates (up to the set speed limit).

If the vehicle ahead slows down or stops, ACC decelerates and—if equipped with stop & go—can bring the car to a halt.

Resuming The system accelerates back to the set speed once the lane ahead is clear.

Example Scenario

You set ACC to 100 km/h and the following distance to 2 seconds.

A car merges ahead traveling at 80 km/h.

ACC detects the vehicle and smoothly reduces your speed to maintain a safe gap.

You set ACC to 100 km/h and the following distance to 2 seconds.

A car merges ahead traveling at 80 km/h.

ACC detects the vehicle and smoothly reduces your speed to maintain a safe gap.

When the lane ahead is clear, ACC returns your car to 100 km/h.

Advantages

Safety: Reduces risk of rear-end collisions.

Convenience: Less driver fatigue on long trips and in traffic jams.

Efficiency: Optimized speed and braking can improve fuel economy.

Limitations

Sensor Limitations: May be affected by weather conditions, dirt, or obstructions.

Not a Substitute for Attention: The driver must remain alert and ready to take control at all times.

Terminology

ACC: Adaptive Cruise Control

ADAS: Advanced Driver Assistance Systems

Advice for Pregnant Women While in a Car

Traveling by car is common during pregnancy, but it’s important to prioritize safety and comfort for both mother and baby. Here’s a quick guide with essential advice:

1. Always Wear Your Seat Belt Properly

Three-Point Seat Belt: Use both lap and shoulder belts.

Lap Belt: Position it under the belly, low on the hips, and across the upper thighs. It should never go across your stomach.

Shoulder Belt: Place it between the breasts and to the side of your belly.

Never Place Belt Behind Back or Under Arm: This reduces its effectiveness and can be dangerous.

2. Adjust Your Seat for Maximum Comfort and Safety

Sit Upright: Maintain a good posture—back straight, shoulders relaxed.

Distance from Steering Wheel/Airbag: Adjust the seat so you’re as far from the dashboard/steering wheel as possible, but still able to drive comfortably.

Tilt Steering Wheel Upwards: If possible, angle the steering wheel towards your chest, not your belly.

Aventro Motors: How to Change a Tyre

Changing a flat tyre is a basic and essential automotive skill for every Aventro Motor car owner. This guide will walk you through:

Steps to change a tyre

Where the spare tyre and toolkit is found in all Aventro models

General tips and safety instructions

Where to Find the Spare Tyre & Toolkit in Aventro Models

Model Type Common Location of Spare Tyre & Toolkit Hatchback Under the boot floor in the rear compartment Sedan Under the boot floor in the trunk SUV Under the boot floor or mounted underneath the rear of the car (All Models) Toolkit is usually secured next to the spare tyre or inside a side
panel of the boot/trunk

Note: All variants (Petrol/Diesel/Electric/Hybrid) follow the same compartment arrangement.

Steps to Change a Tyre

1. Park Safely

Pull over to a safe, flat location away from traffic.

Turn on your hazard lights.

Apply the handbrake.

Place wheel wedges/blocks (if available) to prevent vehicle movement.

2. Gather Tools

metadata.source: C:\Users\fahad\Desktop\Uni\Projects\VoiceKit\business\knowledge_base\Aventro Motors\html\Aventro Motors- How to Change a Tyre.html

text:
Pull over to a safe, flat location away from traffic.

Turn on your hazard lights.

Apply the handbrake.

Place wheel wedges/blocks (if available) to prevent vehicle movement.

2. Gather Tools

You will need: - Spare tyre (found as per table above) - Jack (usually in toolkit) - Lug wrench (in toolkit) - Wheel wedges/blocks (optional) - Vehicle owner’s manual (for reference)

3. Remove the Wheel Cover/Hubcap

If your wheel has a cover, use the flat end of the wrench or the provided lever to gently pry it off.

4. Loosen the Lug Nuts

Use the lug wrench to turn the lug nuts counter-clockwise.

Loosen them slightly – do not remove fully at this stage.

5. Lift the Vehicle with the Jack

Position the jack under the jacking point nearest to the flat tyre. Refer to your owner’s manual for the exact point.

Raise the vehicle until the flat tyre is about 6 inches above the ground.

6. Remove the Lug Nuts and Tyre

Unscrew the lug nuts completely.

Remove the flat tyre and set it aside.

metadata.source: C:\Users\fahad\Desktop\Uni\Projects\VoiceKit\business\knowledge_base\Aventro Motors\html\Aventro Motors- How to Change a Tyre.html

text:
Raise the vehicle until the flat tyre is about 6 inches above the ground.

6. Remove the Lug Nuts and Tyre

Unscrew the lug nuts completely.

Remove the flat tyre and set it aside.

7. Mount the Spare Tyre

Line up the holes and push the spare onto the hub.

Replace the lug nuts and tighten them by hand.

8. Lower the Vehicle

Carefully lower the car with the jack until the tyre touches the ground firmly.

Remove the jack.

9. Tighten the Lug Nuts

Use the lug wrench to tighten the lug nuts in a star pattern to ensure even pressure.

10. Replace the Hubcap or Wheel Cover (if applicable)

Place the hubcap back onto the wheel.

11. Stow Equipment

Put the flat tyre, jack, and tools back in their compartments.

Double check everything is secure.

Safety & Tips

Never change a tyre on a slope or close to traffic.

Use hazard warning triangle if available.

After installation, drive slowly and get the spare tyre pressure checked at the nearest Aventro Service Center.

Best Ways to Maintain Good Mileage

Achieving and maintaining good mileage is essential for saving fuel costs, reducing environmental impact, and ensuring your vehicle’s long-term health. Whether you drive a petrol, diesel, hybrid, or electric car from Aventro Motors, the following practices will help you get the most out of every journey.

1. Regular Maintenance

Follow Service Schedules: Stick to the manufacturer’s recommended service intervals for oil changes, air filter replacements, and other checks.

Use Genuine Parts: Always use genuine Aventro spare parts for optimal performance (e.g., Air Filter, Spark Plug, Oil Filter).

2. Check Tyre Pressure

Maintain Proper Pressure: Under-inflated tyres increase rolling resistance and decrease mileage.

Check Regularly: Inspect tyre pressure at least once a month and before long trips.

3. Drive Smoothly

Avoid Sudden Acceleration or Braking: Rapid changes waste fuel and energy.

5. Reduce Excess Weight

Remove Unnecessary Items: Extra load in the boot or cabin means more work for your engine.

Avoid Unused Racks: Roof boxes or roof racks can reduce aerodynamic efficiency.

6. Monitor Battery Health (For Hybrids & Electrics)

Regular Battery Checks: Ensure the battery pack is in good health to maximize the range.

Use Fast Charging Sparingly: Reserve fast-charging for emergencies to prolong battery life.

7. Use the Right Fuel & Lubricants

Best Ways to Use Your Car AC in All Seasons

For Aventro Motors Car Owners

Your vehicle’s air conditioning (AC) system is vital for comfort and safety throughout the year. Whether it’s cooling in summer, defogging in monsoon, or maintaining a pleasant environment in winter, knowing how to use the AC efficiently will extend system life and enhance your driving experience. Here’s a guide to making the most of your AC system during every season.

Summer: Beat the Heat

1. Ventilate First - Before switching on the AC, roll down the windows and drive for a couple of minutes to expel hot air. - This makes the cabin cool down faster.

2. Use Recirculation Mode - Turn on the AC and set it to “recirculate” once the cabin is cool. - This prevents hot outside air from entering, making the system more effective.

3. Set the Right Temperature - Avoid setting the thermostat to the lowest setting. 22-24°C (72-75°F) is usually comfortable and easier on the compressor.

metadata.source: C:\Users\fahad\Desktop\Uni\Projects\VoiceKit\business\knowledge_base\Aventro Motors\html\Best Ways to Use Your Car AC.html

text:
3. Set the Right Temperature - Avoid setting the thermostat to the lowest setting. 22-24°C (72-75°F) is usually comfortable and easier on the compressor.

4. Regular Maintenance - Clean or replace the cabin air filter. - Get your AC system inspected and refrigerant topped up at an Aventro Service Center before summer starts.

Monsoon: Fight Humidity and Fog

1. Use AC for Defogging - Turn on the AC with the blower directed at the windshield to quickly clear fog. - Use the “fresh air” mode for a few minutes to reduce internal humidity.

2. Don’t Use Recirculate Mode Continuously - Constant recirculation during rains may increase humidity inside, causing more fogging.

3. Keep Windows Closed - Prevent water and more humidity from entering the cabin.

Winter: Comfort with Care

1. Run the AC Regularly - Turn on the AC for at least 10 minutes once a week, even in winter. - This keeps seals lubricated and prevents mold in the system.

Winter: Comfort with Care

1. Run the AC Regularly - Turn on the AC for at least 10 minutes once a week, even in winter. - This keeps seals lubricated and prevents mold in the system.

2. Use AC with Heater for Defogging - Warm air alone may not clear the windshield. - Use the AC and heater together (AC dries the air, heater warms it) for effective demisting.

General Tips for All Seasons

Service Regularly: Schedule professional AC checks at Aventro Service Centers.

Check for Odors: Foul smells may indicate mold – get the filters and system checked.

Avoid Overloading: Don’t overload your car; heavy loads reduce AC efficiency.

Park in Shade: Protect your car from direct sun to reduce AC workload.

Best Ways to Use Your headlamps Based on Road, Traffic, and Climate

Driving conditions in India can vary dramatically depending on location, weather, and traffic density. Your headlamps (often referred to as headlights)—play a crucial role not only for your visibility but for the safety of everyone on the road. This guide from Aventro Motors outlines the best practices for using your headlamps based on distinct road, traffic, and climate scenarios.

1. Urban Roads with Heavy Traffic

Use low beam: High beams can dazzle oncoming drivers and should be avoided in city traffic.

Turn on your headlamps in the evening/low light: Even if street lights are present, using your headlamps enhances visibility.

Hazards & signal lights: Use these for extra safety during sudden traffic halts or in bumper-to-bumper situations.

2. Rural Roads & Highways

Switch to high beam on poorly lit or empty stretches: Offers extended visibility where street lighting is absent.

metadata.source: C:\Users\fahad\Desktop\Uni\Projects\VoiceKit\business\knowledge_base\Aventro Motors\html\Best Ways to Use Your headlamps.html

text:
2. Rural Roads & Highways

Switch to high beam on poorly lit or empty stretches: Offers extended visibility where street lighting is absent.

Dip your beam for oncoming vehicles: Always shift back to low beam to avoid blinding other drivers.

Check for road signs: Many rural roads feature animal crossings or sharp curves—reduce speed and use dipped beams.

3. Foggy or Rainy Weather

Always use low beam: High beams reflect off fog or rain, worsening visibility.

Activate fog lamps if available: These cut through the mist close to the road.

Use hazard lights only when stationary on road shoulder: Do not use hazards while driving as it confuses other road users.

Reduce speed and increase distance: Wet roads mean longer stopping distances.

4. Dusty or Smoggy Conditions

How to Handle “Engine Won’t Start” Issue

When your Aventro vehicle’s engine refuses to start, it can be frustrating. Use this step-by-step guide to help diagnose and resolve the problem, or to gather information before contacting an Aventro Service Center.

1. Check the Basics

Gear Position: Ensure the car is in ‘Park’ (automatic) or ‘Neutral’ (manual).

Steering Lock: Gently turn the steering wheel while turning the key if steering is locked.

Key/Start Button: Switch ignition off and retry. For push-button start, press brake/clutch while starting.

2. Battery Check

Symptoms: No lights/display, slow/absent cranking sounds, clicking noise.

Actions:

Inspect dashboard for dim or no lights.

Try using headlights or infotainment; if dim or off, battery may be the culprit.

If available, try jump-starting with a healthy battery.

For Electric variants: Ensure Battery Pack has adequate charge. Attempt Fast Charging if possible.

3. Fuel System Inspection

If available, try jump-starting with a healthy battery.

For Electric variants: Ensure Battery Pack has adequate charge. Attempt Fast Charging if possible.

3. Fuel System Inspection

Low Fuel/Empty Tank: Check fuel gauge and fill if necessary.

Diesel Vehicles: Ensure there’s no air lock or recent filter change.

Hybrid/Electric: Ensure main battery charge is sufficient.

4. Starter Motor & Electricals

Symptoms: Single click or silence, even with good battery.

Actions:

Check for blown fuses (refer to user manual location).

Test if interior lights stay bright when key is turned; if yes, suspect starter relay/motor.

5. Check Engine Warning Lights

Look for: Engine/Malfunction lights on dashboard.

Action: If warning lights appear, note down symbol/color for service personnel.

6. Listen for Sounds

Rapid Clicking: Battery/starter issues.

Engine Cranking (but not starting): Possible fuel, ignition, or electrical problems.

No Sound at all: Battery, ignition switch, or starter.

Park & Switch Off the Engine

Ensure your car is completely stopped and the engine is turned off.

Engage the parking brake for safety.

Locate the Fuel Knob Release Lever

The fuel knob release lever is typically found:

On the driver’s side floor, near the seat or door.

In some models, it may be on the dashboard or central console.

Pull the Release Lever

Pull up or push the lever labelled with a fuel pump icon.

You may hear a click indicating the fuel lid has been released.

Exit the Car

Step out of the vehicle and go to the side where the fuel lid (fuel door) is located.

Open the Fuel Lid

Gently open the fuel lid.

You’ll now see the fuel knob (fuel cap).

Turn and Remove the Fuel Knob

Twist the fuel knob (cap) anti-clockwise to unscrew it.

Instrument Cluster Warning Alerts

The instrument cluster in Aventro Motors vehicles is designed to inform the driver about the status of various vehicle systems. Each symbol or indicator light provides information on system performance, potential malfunctions, or urgent warnings requiring immediate action.

Below is a list of common warning alerts you may see in Aventro Motors cars, along with their meanings:

1. Engine Warning Light (Check Engine)

Meaning: Indicates a problem with the engine or emissions control system. Immediate diagnosis is recommended.

2. Battery Warning Light

Meaning: The battery is not charging properly. This could signal alternator failure, battery issues, or wiring problems.

3. Oil Pressure Warning Light

Meaning: Low oil pressure detected. Stop the engine and check oil levels to avoid engine damage.

4. Brake System Warning Light

Meaning: Possible issues with the brake system such as low fluid, worn brake pads, or handbrake engaged.

5. ABS Warning Light

4. Brake System Warning Light

Meaning: Possible issues with the brake system such as low fluid, worn brake pads, or handbrake engaged.

5. ABS Warning Light

Meaning: Indicates a malfunction in the Anti-lock Braking System. Normal brakes may function, but ABS will not.

6. Airbag Warning Light

Meaning: There may be a problem with the airbag system; airbags may not deploy in a collision.

7. Coolant Temperature Warning Light

Meaning: Engine is overheating. Stop the vehicle in a safe place and check coolant levels.

8. Transmission Warning Light

Meaning: Transmission malfunction, possible overheating or system fault. Immediate attention required.

9. Tire Pressure Monitoring System (TPMS) Light

Meaning: One or more tires have low pressure or there’s a sensor malfunction.

10. Traction Control Warning Light

Meaning: Indicates that the traction control system is currently in use or there is a system fault.

Lane Keeping Assist System (LKAS): Overview & Functionality

What is Lane Keeping Assist System (LKAS)?

Lane Keeping Assist System (LKAS) is an advanced driver assistance system (ADAS) designed to enhance road safety by helping drivers keep their vehicles within marked lane boundaries. LKAS is commonly found in modern vehicles and acts as a semi-autonomous feature, working alongside the driver to prevent unintentional lane departure.

Why is LKAS Important?

Reduces Accidents: Lane departures are a major cause of road accidents, especially due to driver drowsiness, distraction, or inattention.

Enhances Safety: By consistently monitoring the vehicle’s position, LKAS can help avoid unintended drift into adjacent lanes.

Supports the Driver: LKAS provides gentle steering inputs or alerts, acting as a backup to human oversight.

How Does Lane Keeping Assist System Work?

1. Sensing the Lane

Supports the Driver: LKAS provides gentle steering inputs or alerts, acting as a backup to human oversight.

How Does Lane Keeping Assist System Work?

1. Sensing the Lane

Cameras: Typically, a forward-facing camera mounted near the rear-view mirror scans the road ahead for lane markings (white/yellow lines).

Sensors: Some advanced systems use a combination of cameras, LIDAR, or radar to enhance accuracy in different lighting and weather conditions.

2. Processing the Image

The camera/system detects lane boundaries by analyzing road markings in real-time.

On-board computers determine if the vehicle is unintentionally veering out of its lane.

3. Warning the Driver

If the vehicle starts drifting toward a lane marking without indicating (using a turn signal), the system may give audible or visual warnings (e.g., a beep, steering wheel vibration, or dashboard alert).

4. Active Assistance

4. Active Assistance

If the driver doesn’t respond to the warnings, LKAS can automatically provide gentle steering input to guide the car back toward the center of the lane.

Some systems may also use selective braking on one side of the vehicle to assist in correcting the course.

Key Features

Automatic Steering Correction: Minor, smooth counter-steering to stay centered in the lane.

Customizable Sensitivity: Most systems allow drivers to adjust the responsiveness or can be switched off.

Integrated with Other Systems: Often works alongside Lane Departure Warning (LDW) and Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC).

Limitations & Considerations

Reliant on Lane Markings: LKAS requires clear, visible lane lines; performance may degrade in poor weather, faded markings, or during road construction.

Not a Substitute for Attention: LKAS assists, but the driver must keep hands on the wheel and remain attentive at all times.

Not a Substitute for Attention: LKAS assists, but the driver must keep hands on the wheel and remain attentive at all times.

May Not Operate at All Speeds: Some systems only work above certain speeds (e.g., above 60 km/h).

Typical LKAS Workflow

Vehicle Camera Detects Lane

Control Unit Monitors Position Relative to Lane Marks

If Drift Detected: System Alerts Driver

If No Response: System Gently Steers Vehicle Back to Lane Center

Conclusion

Lane Keeping Assist System is a valuable safety technology that helps prevent unintentional lane departures, reducing the risk of side-swipe collisions and road departure accidents. While it offers significant safety benefits, it is not an autonomous driving system—driver vigilance and control remain essential.

Opening and Closing the Boot

Opening the Boot

There are several ways you can open the boot (trunk) of your Aventro vehicle, depending on the model and features equipped:

1. Manual Release (Lever/Button)

Locate the boot release lever or button inside the vehicle.

Usually found near the driver’s seat or on the driver’s side door panel.

Pull the lever or press the button.

You’ll hear a click indicating the boot is unlocked.

Go to the rear of the vehicle and lift the boot lid upwards to open.

2. Remote Key Fob

Press and hold the boot release button on your vehicle’s remote key fob.

The boot will unlock and, on some models, may open slightly for you to lift.

3. Exterior Button or Handle

With the vehicle unlocked, press the soft-touch button or lift the handle located just above the number plate or under the boot lid.

Lift the boot gently to open.

4. Hands-Free Option (If Equipped)

Lift the boot gently to open.

4. Hands-Free Option (If Equipped)

With the key fob in your possession, stand behind the boot and make a gentle kicking motion under the center of the rear bumper (sensor area).

Wait for a few seconds; the boot will unlatch automatically. Lift to open.

Closing the Boot

1. Manual Closing

Grip the inner handle or any designated area on the inside of the boot lid.

Pull the boot lid down smoothly and press gently until you hear it latch.

2. Electrically Assisted/Tailgate Models (If Equipped)

Press the boot’s close button (located on the edge of the boot lid).

The lid will automatically close and latch securely.

3. Cautions When Closing

Make sure there are no obstructions or luggage sticking out.

Ensure all hands and fingers are away from the boot area before closing.

Do not slam the boot lid; close it with a gentle but firm push.

Ensure all hands and fingers are away from the boot area before closing.

Do not slam the boot lid; close it with a gentle but firm push.

Note: If the boot does not open or close properly, check if the vehicle is in ‘Valet Mode’ or if the child safety lock for the boot is engaged. For electrically operated boots, ensure the battery has sufficient charge.
